OOTDBuy shopping and delivery guides
Trace a Weidian listing, compare size charts, read warehouse photos and follow an OOTDBuy parcel from packing through delivery.
OOTDBuy spreadsheet FAQ
Which link should I save from an OOTDBuy spreadsheet row?

Save the seller listing and the OOTDBuy purchase page. Note the marketplace, item number and selected option text. If the agent link later opens an empty page, the original listing gives you a way to check whether the seller still offers that option.
Can I use a catalogue photo to find a missing product?

Open Image search from the navigation and upload a crop showing one item. Compare distinctive features in the results, then open the seller listing and check the identifier. A close visual match can come from a different seller.
What if two almost identical jackets appear in search?

Compare pocket position, zip pulls and panel seams in the detail pictures. Then compare seller, item ID and option text. Keep both links until you can explain which listing matches the jacket you want.
Does a copied Weidian link remember my size?
Reopen the copied link and check the selected options. Keep the exact colour and size text alongside it. Some links identify a listing with several choices and reopen at its default selection.
How can I tell a style photograph from a detail photograph?

Select two styles in succession and watch which image changes with the choice. Use that image to identify the option. Use the gallery below it to inspect features such as fasteners or lining, and verify which style those gallery pictures depict.
Which number should I use to compare two Weidian links?
Compare the itemID on the seller pages. Matching numbers identify the same listing on Weidian. Also compare the size, colour and package choice because multiple options can share that number.
Does a missing style photograph mean that colour is sold out?

Check whether the exact colour can be selected on the live seller or agent page. A catalogue can have a name for a colour without having a picture for it. Use the live option status when deciding whether to order.
Why can the lowest displayed price change when I choose a style?

Check which option the initial price describes. A listing may include a single accessory, a garment and a set. After selecting your option, read the unit, quantity and subtotal together before comparing prices.
How do I check whether a listing includes both pieces of a set?

Read the seller option text for the top, bottom or complete set. Save the wording and inspect the order summary. A model wearing two pieces in one picture does not establish that the seller supplies both.
What does a historical QC picture tell me?

It can show visible details of a unit photographed earlier. Match the marketplace listing, option and identifying features before using it. For a decision about your current order, ask to see the item tied to your order number.
Can I judge colour from one warehouse picture?

Look for a neutral item in the same frame and compare several views. If colour determines whether you will keep the item, ask for a closer view under neutral light with the option label visible. Screen settings and lighting can change its appearance.
How should I compare a flat chest measurement to my own shirt?

Lay a shirt that fits flat, without stretching it. Measure from underarm seam to underarm seam. Compare with a photo using the same endpoints and units. A chart giving chest circumference uses a different measurement.
What makes a tape-measure photo usable?

Both endpoints, the zero mark and the reading should be visible in one view. Check that the tape follows the requested path and lies flat. A close-up of a number alone cannot show which part was measured.
How do I check a shoe-size label?

Ask for a clear picture of the label and compare the exact sizing system and printed size with the order. If length matters, define whether you need removable insole length or another measurement before requesting a photo.
Which pictures help when a set is missing a piece?

Save the seller option description, your order confirmation and one picture showing everything received together. Identify the missing piece by name and contact OOTDBuy from the order while the item can still be inspected.
Which price should I use for a budget in my own currency?

Start with the live price for your chosen option and quantity. Record the original currency, conversion rate and time of comparison. At payment, check the currency and total on the actual checkout screen.
Does the item price include international delivery?

Read the item checkout and parcel quote separately. Record any seller-to-warehouse delivery charge on the purchase side. For the outbound parcel, check the destination, route, packing and services shown in the current quote.
What should I record when comparing parcel estimates?

Use the same destination, weight, dimensions, units and contents on both estimates. Save the route name and included services beside each result. A cheaper figure based on a smaller assumed box is a different comparison.
How do I decide whether to keep the original retail box?

Write down what the box does for this item, such as supporting a fragile shape or keeping pieces together. Compare the available packing options and ask about effects on return eligibility before authorizing disposal.
Where should I check the storage deadline?

Check the warehouse entry for the specific item and consult Storage in the OOTDBuy Help Center. For items that arrived on different dates, record the deadline for each entry before waiting for the rest of the order.
Which tracking number belongs to the outbound shipment?
Match the number on your international parcel record to the carrier shown there. Keep the seller's domestic delivery number separately. Its delivery scan can refer to arrival at the warehouse.
How do I report damage after delivery?

Keep the parcel label and packaging. Photograph the outer box, internal protection, affected item and damaged area. Send the parcel reference and a description through OOTDBuy's after-sales channel and check its current reporting conditions.
Where can I check OOTDBuy return, inspection and delivery rules?

Open the official Help Center. The Shopping Agent Guide covers returns, Warehouse & After-sale covers inspection and storage, and Delivery covers packaging and charges. For an individual order, include its reference when contacting support.
How to match OOTDBuy QC photos to the variant you want

A familiar photograph can lead you to the right jacket and the wrong version of it. Before using a warehouse picture to choose a size, colour or seller, trace the picture back to a listing and work out exactly which option it shows.
Start with the decision the photograph needs to answer

Suppose you have saved a dark jacket from an OOTDBuy spreadsheet. The photographs show a two-way zip and a short body. The live listing offers several dark options, and the English translation gives two of them almost the same name. You care about the zip because you cycle to work. A picture showing that feature on one jacket is useful, but there are two separate questions to answer. Did it come from the listing you plan to use? Does it show the option that will appear on your order?

Write the decision down in one sentence before collecting images. For this jacket it might be “I need the short black version with the zip that opens from the hem.” That description tells you which evidence to seek. A close photograph of the neck label might confirm the marked size, yet contribute nothing to the zip question. A full front view with both sliders visible would help. If fit also matters, handle it as a separate measurement question so that one convincing detail does not stand in for the rest.
Trace the reference back to the seller listing

Open the spreadsheet result and save the original marketplace link beside the OOTDBuy link. Write down the seller name and the marketplace item identifier if you can see them. On a Weidian item URL, look for the value of itemID. Compare it on the two seller links you are investigating. Matching values on Weidian establish that the links point to the same listing. An item number taken from another marketplace has no such meaning, even if the digits happen to look familiar.

If all you have is a screenshot, crop to one garment and use image search to find candidates. Leave enough of the outline to show the hem and collar. A crop of a large chest graphic can return other garments carrying that print. Open each promising result and compare construction details that a seller would find harder to change with different styling. Count the pocket openings, find where the shoulder seam ends and look at how the zip is attached. A visual match is a lead. Save the link as unconfirmed until you have connected it to the seller or resolved the uncertainty.
Identify the option inside the listing

Copy the option wording as the seller presents it, including any model code or short suffix. Keep the original text beside your own description. When a listing uses “black A” and “black B,” a translation that displays only “black” loses the distinction that controls what the seller dispatches. Reopen your saved link in a separate tab. See whether it opens with the option already selected. If it resets, save a screenshot of the selection and choose the option again at checkout.

Change one selector at a time and watch what happens. Start with the colour while keeping the size fixed. Then change the size. Does the main picture change when you select the shorter jacket, or does the same promotional photograph remain for all choices? Look for a written specification that confirms the feature you need. If the selector switches between jacket only and jacket with trousers, check the unit and the subtotal too. The fact that a model wears the complete outfit in a photograph tells you how it was styled.
Choose a useful historical QC photograph

A QC finder or a spreadsheet gallery may contain pictures from previous orders. Look for a reference that exposes the detail you are testing. For the two-way zip, the lower slider and its orientation matter more than a high-resolution picture of the fabric. Inspect the whole sequence when one is available. A wide shot establishes which item is on the table. A closer view can then show what is attached to it. A cropped image shared without that context is weaker evidence.

Read any option or size information attached to the reference. When the size is missing, use the picture only for features it actually shows. It may establish that a jacket photographed for this listing had a zip of a particular design. It cannot tell you the chest width of the medium you are considering. Keep a short note beside the link, such as “lower zip visible, colour label unreadable, size unknown.” This preserves the value of the photograph without silently turning unknown details into expectations about your own order.
Check measurements with a comparison garment

Choose a jacket that fits over the layer you intend to wear. Close it, lay it flat and smooth out folds without stretching the fabric. Measure underarm to underarm across the body. Then measure back length from a named starting point, for example the centre seam where the collar joins the back, down to the hem. Write down both endpoints and the unit. If a seller measures length from the highest point of the shoulder, take a second measurement from that point before comparing the numbers.

Imagine that your own flat width is 56 centimetres and a chart lists a chest of 112 centimetres. Those figures could describe similar widths if the chart gives a whole garment circumference. If the chart describes a body measurement instead, the comparison changes completely. Read the diagram or ask how the measurement was taken. This is an illustrative calculation. For your actual order, use the chart attached to the exact version you selected and a photograph with the tape visible if precise fit will decide whether you keep it.
Request a photograph that resolves the uncertainty

Instead of asking for “more QC,” explain the observation you need. For example, “Please photograph the entire front of the black short jacket in order [reference], with the zip closed and both sliders visible. I am checking whether it opens from the hem.” For a measurement, specify that the item should lie flat and identify both tape endpoints. Someone inspecting the photo should be able to see the zero mark and the final reading in the same frame. A close-up showing only a number leaves room for different interpretations.

Use the order channel for your own purchase and check the current options for inspection or additional pictures there. The OOTDBuy Help Center groups inspection information under warehouse and after-sales topics. It also has separate purchasing and returns guidance. Read the applicable instructions for your item before assuming that a particular view is included, available, or sufficient for a return. Keep your question short enough that the person handling the item can answer it with a specific picture or a direct observation.
Make the decision against the actual order

Put the selected seller option, your order confirmation and the pictures of the received item side by side. Work through your original requirements individually. The option text can confirm what you ordered. The front view can show the zip design. The measurement photo can support the fit comparison. If an important detail contradicts the order, identify that precise difference in a message while the item is still available for inspection. Save the original listing evidence, particularly if the seller has since edited the options.

Close the comparison with a decision you can explain in one line. “The order shows short black, the lower slider is visible, and the measured back length matches my comparison jacket” is a reason to proceed. “The reference looks right, but my item has only been photographed in its bag” leaves a clear question to resolve. A written decision also helps when two similar pieces arrive together. Later, when you open the parcel, the item reference, selected option and accepted photographs still tell you which garment each decision concerned.
Keep the right evidence when an OOTDBuy spreadsheet listing changes

A seller can update the options behind a saved link while the photograph in your spreadsheet still looks familiar. The important question is what changed between the version you saw and the version you are being asked to buy. A short record made at the right time lets you answer that question even if the old page disappears.
Choose a useful starting point

Imagine saving a brown shoulder bag on Monday because the longer strap is included. You return on Friday and the photograph looks the same. There are now options called “bag” and “bag with accessories.” You remember the strap quite clearly, but do you remember whether it came with both options? A screenshot of the model wearing the bag cannot settle this. The picture shows a possible way of using it. The selected option and its written contents tell you what the seller was offering. Start a record when a feature like that influences your decision.

Take a view that includes the option name, its selected state and the amount for that selection. If these appear on separate parts of a mobile screen, take two pictures and give them the same short reference. Add one sentence describing the reason for saving the find. For the bag, write “long strap included in brown option,” provided that the wording actually supports it. If the wording never mentions the strap, write “long strap in model picture; inclusion unknown.” The second note is equally valuable because it tells you what to ask.
Keep the marketplace identity separate from the agent view

Keep the seller link as well as the link that opens the item on OOTDBuy. Name the marketplace and seller so that you can recognize the source if a sharing service shortens or reformats the URL. When there is a visible marketplace item identifier, record it together with the marketplace name. A number on its own is a poor search key across services. Include the option wording in its original language, especially a short suffix or version code which might disappear in a translation.

A record need not be elaborate. One row can carry the date, the two links, the item identifier, the option and the price in its original currency. Put the reason for saving the item in the last cell. If you save ten rows in an evening, the final cell is usually the one you will want a week later. “Brown bag” makes you repeat the search. “Long strap shown; waiting for seller to confirm inclusion” lets you pick up the decision where you left it.
Distinguish a changed option from a changed price

Reopen the saved source and select the same option again before comparing amounts. A lower figure shown before selection may belong to a smaller size, a spare strap or another item sold under that listing. Select the original quantity as well. If the seller has introduced a quantity tier, a three-unit offer can show a different unit price from a single unit even when the item itself is unchanged. Record the actual selection that produced the new amount.

For example, suppose your saved note says “one brown bag with strap, 120 yuan.” The live page shows 95 yuan as soon as it opens, then 125 yuan after you choose the version with strap. The comparable change in this example is five yuan. The apparent saving of 25 yuan depends on a different selection. Before changing your budget, check the seller's description of what comes with the 95-yuan option. The numbers here illustrate how to make the comparison; use the values displayed for your own item.
Deal with an option that has disappeared

Sometimes an old choice vanishes entirely. Avoid silently substituting the nearest translation. An option called “second generation” may be a replacement for the earlier design, or the seller may be selling two constructions under a familiar name. Open its own detail description, size table and pictures. Look for the feature that mattered in your original decision, such as strap length, buckle type or the position of an interior pocket. Record whether each visible difference would change your choice.

If the product could still work, ask one answerable question. “Does the current brown bag option include the detachable long strap shown in the fourth photograph?” gives the seller or agent something to check. “Is this the same bag?” can mean identical colour, size, material or included accessories. If the exact version is essential, say that an alternative requires your approval. This matters particularly for a manual order where the short option name might otherwise look close enough to use.
Keep chronology when purchase has already happened

Once you place an order, keep the order confirmation as a separate record. It describes the selection associated with your transaction. A seller page saved after purchase belongs in a later column. Replacing your original screenshot with a current one can erase the very difference you are trying to explain. Mark the time and timezone if two changes took place close together. Do not put private payment details in a public spreadsheet shared with other buyers.

When the item reaches the warehouse, match the received piece to the order. The current listing can help you identify what the seller is selling today, but the issue you need to resolve concerns what you ordered and what arrived. Show those records side by side. If the problem is an omitted strap, a view of the bag with all wrapping and pocket contents laid out provides clearer evidence than another screenshot of the seller's cover picture. Keep a note of where the evidence came from.
Update a shared spreadsheet without erasing the earlier decision

For a personal list, a change note can be brief. For a shared list, use neutral wording a second reader can verify. Write “seller page checked Tuesday; long strap now has a separate selector” and include the current link. A statement that the seller shipped the wrong item requires evidence about a particular purchase. Everyone else using the sheet needs to know which listing and option you checked, and whether the issue concerned a saved row or a completed order.

If a replacement seller link appears, give it its own row. Match the new seller, item number, selected contents and relevant measurements independently. A gallery can reuse the same studio images across several offers. Replacing the URL in the original cell while keeping the old size notes, price and QC references creates a record that looks complete but describes more than one offer. Link the two rows with a short note explaining why the second one is under consideration.
Decide whether the change matters

Some changes require little additional work. A corrected title can leave the seller, item number, option specification and price intact. A new accessory selector, a different size chart or an unexplained jump between quantities is worth checking before purchase. State your decision in terms of the feature that matters to you. “Will buy the current option if the long strap measures at least the length of my existing strap” is easier to act on than a general feeling that the new listing seems different.

For an issue with an order already placed, consult the purchasing or after-sales information in the official OOTDBuy Help Center and use the order reference in your inquiry. For a find you have only bookmarked, you can simply leave the row pending. A careful record should save time on both outcomes. It should let you purchase a changed listing confidently when the evidence matches, and walk away from an unresolved change without having to reconstruct the entire search.
The OOTDBuy listing has a colour name but no photo. Which option should you choose?

You tap an olive swatch and the photograph stays black. That tells you something about the page, but it leaves two important questions open. Does the seller actually offer an olive version, and does “olive” describe the shade you have in mind? Treat availability and appearance as separate checks. An empty image slot answers neither of them.
Find out which image is missing

Open the row on OOTDBuy Grid, note the exact option name and compare two or three colour choices. Watch the small option image as well as the large picture. A selector can have a thumbnail while the top of the page continues to show a generic cover. On a phone, changing an option lower down the page may leave the photograph outside the viewport. Scroll back once and see what actually changed. Record the option that remained selected after the change.

Next, distinguish an absent picture from one that failed to load. If all product pictures are blank, try the seller listing before drawing conclusions about any particular option. If a dozen swatches have images and just one lacks one, note that specific gap. For a purchase decision, the practical question is whether you can see a photograph explicitly linked to your choice. The reason a thumbnail is missing can wait unless it stops you from selecting the item at all.
Read the complete option, including the suffix

A seller can group colour, finish and construction into one field. “Green B” might identify a particular fabric, length or hardware combination. A translation that displays only “green” makes two choices look interchangeable. Copy the original wording, preserve any letters or digits and compare the position of that option on the seller page. A screenshot that shows your click in context is more helpful than a cut-out image of a coloured circle.

Suppose a listing offers a grey bag with silver fittings and another grey bag with dark fittings. Both use one wide photograph of a person wearing the bag. Your real choice concerns the hardware. Look for an option code or text specifically naming the fittings. A grey thumbnail cannot answer the question even if it loads perfectly. Reducing the decision to a concrete feature gives a support agent or seller something specific to confirm.
Check stock independently of the gallery

Open the current seller or agent purchase view and choose the complete combination you would buy. A colour can be listed at the product level but unavailable in the size or finish you need. If the form changes the quantity back to zero, clears the size, or shows a separate stock message, read that message before continuing. An enabled colour button does not by itself establish that a particular combination can be ordered today.

When recording the result, use wording that distinguishes supply from missing evidence. “Olive, medium selectable; no image tied to that option” is much more useful than “olive missing.” A friend reading the second note cannot tell whether the item sold out, the site failed to display a picture or the seller never photographed it. If the purchase is time-sensitive, confirm availability through the current order interface. A record you made yesterday describes yesterday's selection.
Use other photographs for the details they actually show

A detail gallery can answer questions about the shape of a collar, the location of a pocket or the type of fastening even when it cannot confirm colour. Look for a feature that connects a photograph to the exact option, such as a label with the seller's code in the same frame. If the photograph came from a different listing or has only a translation in the filename, give it less weight. Keep alternative listings as leads so you do not accidentally attach their photos to your order.

Historical warehouse pictures can help you decide what to ask next. A picture of an older olive jacket, for example, can reveal that a drawcord or lining uses an unexpected contrasting colour. Before using it to choose the current jacket, check whether the seller, item identifier and option correspond. Even when they match, a picture of an earlier unit cannot identify the unit a seller will send for your order. Keep the date and the source beside the picture.
Compare shades under sensible conditions

A screen is a poor measuring instrument for colour. Warm light can give a grey fabric a beige cast, while a reflective surface can look brighter where it faces a lamp. If you are matching an existing piece, decide first how much a shade difference matters. A tonal outfit may allow a range. A replacement part intended to sit next to its mate may require a closer match. The acceptable difference depends on your purpose.

For a practical request, ask for two views of the same item in the same setting. One can show the complete object beside its option label; the other can show the relevant surface under neutral light. A familiar neutral object can help interpret a colour cast, though it cannot calibrate your display or guarantee agreement with the item in your hand. Avoid asking someone to decide whether it is “exactly like my screen.” Ask them to confirm the seller's colour code and photograph the actual unit.
Make your purchase note unambiguous

Consider this example message. “I want the olive option marked G2, size medium. The spreadsheet thumbnail is empty. Please use G2 only and contact me if this version is unavailable. The black cover picture is not my choice.” It gives the reader a selection, a size and an instruction for an exception. If the seller uses a different label, quote its wording instead of inventing your own code. Keep the screenshot with the note in case the order page later changes.

If you would accept an alternative, define the limit in the same message. “Silver or grey fittings are acceptable; please ask before substituting the black bag” is a different instruction from “any similar colour is fine.” Check how the agent actually records the note and selection before paying. Save a copy of the confirmed option. The note and the selected line should agree; a note asking for olive beside a paid line for black creates avoidable uncertainty.
Review the received unit, then close the decision

When warehouse pictures are available, open the entry for your purchase and compare its label with the saved order. Examine the full item before zooming into highlights or shadows. If two units are present, identify which one carries your size label. A close photograph of a zipper can show the hardware but leave the garment's identity unclear. Request the single missing view that would actually change your decision rather than accumulating more pictures of the same angle.

If the label contradicts the confirmed order, save both pieces of evidence and consult the official OOTDBuy help information for the stage of the purchase. If the label matches yet the shade remains uncertain, say so accurately. You might accept that uncertainty for a casual item, or ask about available options before international dispatch. The outcome should follow the original purpose: buying a named version, matching a wardrobe piece, or avoiding a particular finish. The missing photograph becomes manageable once you know which question remains unanswered.
How to save a Weidian link from OOTDBuy without losing the style you chose

You send a friend the link to the navy sweatshirt in size large. They open it and see a white sweatshirt in small. The link may still point to the correct product. What failed to travel with it was the selection. Save a listing address and a short option record together, then test the result in a fresh tab before you rely on it for an order.
Decide which destination the recipient needs

A product card can reasonably offer more than one destination. The original marketplace listing helps you check the seller, options and description. An agent purchase link helps a buyer open the item with the intended purchasing service. The address of a catalogue page helps someone retrace where the find appeared. Each one answers a different request. When another person asks for the Weidian link, give them the seller address and identify the agent link separately if they also want that.

Copy the link attached to the relevant product rather than the address of the results page where you found it. A category or search URL can show a different order of results tomorrow. Avoid copying a picture address from the gallery. A picture address opens an image; it cannot tell the recipient who sells the item, which size is available or what the current price is. Open what you copied and look at the destination before sharing it.
Read the listing identity from the opened page

Weidian product links often carry an itemID parameter. Record the marketplace and its itemID together where the link exposes it. Keep a separate field for a shop identifier, an agent order number or your own spreadsheet row. These numbers may all appear in an ordering workflow, but they identify different things. If a recipient asks why two versions open to the same item, first see whether both links have the same marketplace item identifier. They may simply be options within one offer.

A short sharing link may redirect before the seller page opens. Let it reach its destination and check the shop and product shown there. Keep the original link if it is the only one you can verify. Making up a shorter address by deleting everything after a question mark can remove the very identifier that tells the site what to load. If you want a cleaner link, compare the full destinations yourself after the edit. Preserve the tested address in your private notes.
Build a minimum option record

For most clothing finds, record the colour or version text, selected size and quantity. If there is a seller code beside the translation, keep it. Add the unit whenever a set or pack is involved. “Two blue” leaves open whether you mean two single shirts, two sets or the second blue version in the selector. “Blue B, large, quantity two, one shirt per unit” gives another person a selection they can reproduce and a quantity they can check at checkout.

A screenshot can supplement the note but it is not a substitute for selectable text. On a phone, a long option may be truncated with an ellipsis. Tap through to the full description or save a wider view if available. Attach the screenshot to the same note as the seller URL. If you send images and links separately in a long chat, mark them with a short shared reference like “navy sweatshirt B.” The recipient can then keep the correct screenshot if you later send an alternative.
Test the link without your existing selection

Open a fresh tab and paste the copied URL. See which colour, size and package choice are actually selected. Repeat the check with a second version from the same listing. If both links reopen with the same default, the link is useful at the listing level and your note must carry the option. If the URL does restore the selected variant, keep the text anyway. It gives the recipient a human-readable check if the seller edits the options later.

Check the price after reproducing the selection. Imagine a sweatshirt page that also offers a drawstring accessory. A link opening to the accessory may show a dramatically lower starting figure than the amount attached to the sweatshirt. Record the selected unit price with its currency, and say when you saw it. A recipient can then tell whether the apparent discrepancy comes from a default option or a change in the offer. Use the live checkout amount when paying.
Keep the product identity through a change of agent

Suppose the recipient wants to use OOTDBuy, while the person who originally shared the find used another agent. Start from the saved marketplace listing. Open it through the desired purchasing route and compare the resulting seller, item and available options. Use the colour and size note you recorded, paying particular attention to shortened translations. If two labels now look identical, the source codes or original wording can resolve the ambiguity.

An agent view that shows only a generic title or one photo leaves missing information. Before submitting a manual request, write down the complete purchase instruction and identify the one thing that still needs confirmation. For example, “Please order the navy B version, size L, two single shirts. Contact me if this version has sold out.” Avoid instructions like “same as photo” if the photo shows a model wearing multiple products. It leaves the person placing the order to decide what is included.
Handle a changed or unavailable seller page

A dead link deserves a status entry of its own. Give the date, the marketplace and the item identifier if known. When a seller offers a replacement link, compare the new seller name, size chart, option description and current price. If the replacement has a different item number, save it on a new row. Historical pictures under the old row may still illustrate a design feature but cannot establish what the new seller will supply.

If the page loads and your exact option is greyed out, distinguish that case from a dead listing. Write “page available, navy B in L currently unavailable” rather than marking the entire find as broken. A second buyer looking for medium can still check that option. A buyer who needs large now knows what to ask about. The difference also matters when updating a shared spreadsheet: deleting an entire row can hide other choices that remain usable.
Give the recipient a usable handoff

A concise handoff can fit in one message. Include the tested seller link, the intended agent link if requested, the option text, size, quantity and anything that requires confirmation. Keep private order numbers out of a public sheet. For a personal purchase, put the order reference in a separate private record once the transaction is placed. That division lets a shared link remain useful to other readers without revealing which order belongs to whom.

Before you close the tab, ask whether a stranger could reproduce your choice from the material you saved. They should know where the listing comes from, which option to select and which parts are still uncertain. If the answer depends on remembering that “the second picture meant the long version,” add those words now. This final minute of checking is especially worthwhile for a multi-style Weidian listing. It makes the copied link a practical buying reference, even on a device that has never opened it before.
Comparing two OOTDBuy size charts when neither uses your usual measurements

Two jackets look equally suitable in an OOTDBuy spreadsheet. In one listing the medium has a chest of 58; in the other the large has a bust of 116. Those figures could describe nearly the same garment. They could also describe entirely different things. Before choosing between them, identify who or what was measured, which two points the tape touched and which garment needs to fit underneath.
Pick a reference you actually wear

Take a jacket from your wardrobe that fits the way you want these purchases to fit. Try it on with the layer you expect to wear. Raise your arms, zip the front and sit down. Write down the one feature that feels right and one you might change. Perhaps its chest is comfortable over a sweater but its cuffs ride up. This note makes your comparison more useful than a list of measurements taken without a purpose. You are choosing a fit for an activity, not trying to duplicate every dimension.

Lay the reference flat on a firm surface. Empty the pockets, straighten the seams and close the garment as you did when trying it on. Keep the tape level without pulling the fabric taut. Measure once, lift the tape, then measure again. If your two readings differ, note what moved. A thick fleece can bunch at the underarm, while an unfastened front can spread wider the second time. Resolve that small uncertainty at home before interpreting a difference of a centimetre in a chart.
Identify garment dimensions and body recommendations

Read the headings and the accompanying diagram as a pair. A body chart recommends a size for a person with certain measurements. A garment chart describes the piece that person will wear. You cannot compare a body chest circumference directly with the width of a jacket laid on a table. Fabric, lining, cut and room for movement separate those values. If the listing does not tell you which type of chart you are looking at, keep that field unresolved.

Take a working example. Your reference jacket is 58 cm from underarm to underarm. Listing A gives a flat width of 57 cm at the same points. Listing B gives a finished garment circumference of 116 cm, explicitly measured around the chest. Roughly doubling the flat reference gives 116 cm, so B looks closer on this dimension. That does not establish identical fit. Thick material, curved seams and different armholes can make the simple doubling rule imprecise. The two chart values are now interpretable, which is the point of the exercise.
Match the length definition before comparing numbers

Length is often the measurement that exposes an otherwise attractive comparison. One seller may start at the high shoulder beside the neck; another may measure down the centre back from the collar seam. A decorative collar or a dropped rear hem makes the difference especially noticeable. Look for the start and finish in the seller's diagram, then take both measurements on your reference jacket. Label them with the endpoints instead of keeping a single number called length.

Imagine you record 68 cm from the high shoulder and 65 cm down the centre back. A listing showing a centre-back length of 66 cm is about one centimetre longer by the corresponding method. Comparing it with 68 cm would lead you to call it shorter. With a cropped jacket the mistaken conclusion can affect whether the hem clears your waistband. If the listing omits the starting point, ask for the method rather than guessing which convention the seller used.
Account for shoulder shape when comparing sleeves

Put a conventional shoulder jacket beside a drop-shoulder sweatshirt. The sleeve seam starts at a different point on the arm, so comparable cuff placement can come from very different sleeve lengths in a chart. A raglan piece creates another complication because its seam runs diagonally toward the neck. Compare like construction where possible. When two pieces differ, a neck-to-cuff measurement with explicit endpoints can provide a more useful common reference than the sleeve seam alone.

To check a photograph, trace the path of the tape with your eye. Is the cuff turned up? Is the sleeve bent or stretched? Does the zero mark sit on the seam you requested? A close crop of the final number can be completely legible and still answer the wrong question. If you have only one additional view available, request a single frame showing the entire path. Include the size and colour in the request so the photographer measures the item you plan to keep.
Read a set as two garments

A sweatshirt-and-trousers set may use one size selector even though the top and bottom have separate charts. Compare both pieces before choosing. For trousers, decide which measurement matters most for your use: relaxed waist, seat width, rise, inseam or the opening that must pass over your shoe. A seller's flat relaxed waist tells you something different from a stretched maximum. Ask whether a quoted pair of values represents a measurement range or the ends of two different sizes.

Suppose the top in medium matches your reference and the trousers in medium are too short. Moving to large may increase the trousers' length while making the top wider than you like. Write these two outcomes on separate lines. Then check whether the seller allows mixed sizes for that particular option. A model photograph showing two pieces together gives no answer about the order form. If mixed sizing is unavailable, decide which compromise you are willing to wear before committing to the set.
Convert once and keep the original figures

If your measuring tape uses inches and the seller uses centimetres, convert your own reference once using 2.54 centimetres per inch. A 22.5-inch flat chest is 57.15 cm. Keeping 57.2 cm for comparison is usually more practical than repeatedly converting a chart column and rounding it to whole inches. Retain the original reading as well. It allows you to spot a transcription error if one result seems far outside the range of your other clothing.

Do not give a chart more precision than the measurement supports. A difference of a few millimetres should be considered alongside the seller's stated tolerance, your own repeat readings and the behaviour of the fabric. If no tolerance is given, avoid inventing one. A thick quilted piece can have a generous external measurement and feel snug inside. Use garment construction and the intended underlayer to decide when a close comparison still leaves an important question open.
Write the buying decision while the charts are visible

A useful note identifies the chosen option, reference garment, measurement method and remaining uncertainty. For example: “Considering listing B, large, black. Finished chest is closest to my winter jacket. Centre-back length confirmed. Ask for neck-to-cuff because the shoulders are cut differently.” The note lets you return to the listing without repeating every calculation. Save the chart image or seller description alongside it, particularly if several versions share one product page.

When the warehouse entry is available, compare the actual item against the decision you recorded. Use the OOTDBuy order channel if you need an item-specific measurement, and review the current inspection information in the Help Center. You have finished the comparison when you can explain why one size meets your needs and which evidence supports that conclusion. If a necessary measurement remains missing, keeping the row pending is a perfectly defensible result.
Reading an OOTDBuy product gallery when the photographs tell different stories

One frame shows a backpack with an outside zip pocket, a close-up shows a smooth front, and another picture includes a small shoulder strap. All three images appear beneath the same product title. Which bag are you actually looking at? A gallery often combines several kinds of evidence. Read it in a deliberate order and use the gaps to formulate a question about the precise version you intend to buy.
Begin with the object outline

Find the clearest complete view of the item. Look at its shape, opening, panel lines and the way accessories attach. Use a few fixed landmarks that remain visible even if the camera angle changes. On a backpack those might be the number of zip tracks, the shape of the main flap and the position of the strap anchors. On a jacket you might choose the collar, front fastening and lower pockets. These landmarks give the other photographs something to connect to.

Write a literal description before judging quality. “Two zip tracks meet above a rectangular front panel” captures evidence another reader can check. “Looks like the premium version” puts an interpretation ahead of the details. This pays off when the same gallery includes more than one release. You can match a close-up of a zip pull to the bag with the corresponding track arrangement. If the landmarks cannot be seen in the close-up, leave its relationship to the main picture open.
Read option photographs as part of the selector

Select the colour or model you want and observe which pictures change with it. Keep the selected text visible when you save a reference. A seller may use one promotional hero image for the whole listing and reserve the smaller swatch image for the exact option. Alternatively, the swatches may all use the same picture with different written codes. In either case, changing the selection is a useful test because it shows whether the interface associates a particular picture with an option.

Consider a bag listing with compact and full-size versions. Both versions might have the same colourway and nearly identical front styling. A picture that changes when you switch from black to green says little about which size has been selected. Toggle only the size and check again. If no photograph changes, read the written dimensions for the chosen size. A photograph of the bag worn by a model may offer context, but the model's proportions and camera perspective make it unsuitable as the only size evidence.
Work outward from a detail picture

A close-up can reveal stitching, texture or the shape of a fastening. To relate it to the item, look for an intermediate view showing where that detail sits. A picture of an isolated clasp is weaker evidence for a detachable strap than a view showing the clasp attached to the strap and its attachment ring on the bag. If the strap determines whether you will buy, look for the option description listing it among the supplied pieces. A gallery can show an optional accessory for styling.

Zoom only as far as the image resolution supports. Sharpening or enlarging a low-resolution crop cannot reveal a character on an unreadable label with confidence. The same applies to texture. A reflection on a smooth coated surface can resemble a crease, while compression artefacts can make a straight seam look jagged. Mark the observation and ask for a clear view of that area if it would change your purchase decision. A precise request is more useful than a verdict from a handful of pixels.
Identify graphics and diagrams

A dimension drawing, colour chart or instructions panel can appear between photographs with little explanation. Check the labels around it. The diagram may apply to the whole family, a named model or the packaging rather than the product. In the backpack example, outside dimensions do not give the exact dimensions of an internal laptop sleeve. Padding, rounded corners and an opening narrower than the body all matter. Ask for sleeve width and usable opening if you need to carry a specific object.

If you compare a drawing to a product photograph, make sure the orientation agrees. The length shown along the bottom of a bag is different from the usable internal depth. A side view with a gusset folded inward may understate how the bag looks when filled. Keep the seller's named measurement and unit with your note. If a graphic is in another language, retain the original label alongside the translation so you can revisit it if the interpretation seems inconsistent.
Separate historical QC from seller presentation

A warehouse reference may show an ordinary unit under simple light and make proportions easier to understand. Check its source and any accompanying item or option information. An old picture attached to a marketplace identifier remains a record of that photographed unit. It does not establish which option the seller sends now. If the website does not identify a photograph as a warehouse image, describe it simply as a gallery photograph. A plain background alone cannot identify who took it.

Suppose a historical shot shows a removable organizer inside the backpack. The selected seller option describes only the bag. The right question is whether the organizer belongs to that option today. A second image of another customer's organizer might confirm that the accessory exists without answering whether it is included. Record the strongest conclusion you can actually support, then ask for confirmation of the missing part of the claim.
Make a contradiction list you can act on

You do not need to annotate every image. List the contradictions that affect your requirements. For the backpack you might record three: the outside pocket appears only in the studio picture, the dark green option has no front view, and the sleeve drawing has no internal width. Beside each, identify the simplest evidence that would settle it. A front photograph of the selected bag answers two of those questions at once. A measurement of the sleeve opening addresses the third.

Send the request with the seller option text and a description of the relevant location. “Please show the front of the dark green full-size bag, then the width of its laptop sleeve opening with the tape visible” gives the reader a reproducible task. If the item is in your order, add its reference in the private OOTDBuy order channel. For available inspection services and the stage at which you can request them, consult the official Help Center and the current order interface.
Use the gallery when the item arrives

When reviewing pictures of your own unit, bring back the same landmarks and the same contradiction list. Match the order option first. Then decide whether the photographs answer your essential requirements. A visible outside zip answers the pocket question; it does not establish laptop clearance. A sleeve measurement can support your size decision but does not settle whether a detachable organizer is included. Keep each conclusion with the evidence that supports it.

At the end you should be able to explain the choice in plain terms. You might decide that the exact shade matters little, that a usable sleeve opening matters a great deal, and that the organizer can be purchased separately. Someone with different priorities can reasonably reach another conclusion from the same photographs. A good reading of an OOTDBuy gallery gives you that freedom. It turns a long, sometimes inconsistent collection of pictures into a short set of observations that actually changes what you do.
How to document a damaged item for an OOTDBuy after-sales request

You open a parcel and find a crack across the handle of a mug. The carton has a dent, yet the mug was wrapped well enough that the dent may be unrelated. You do not have to decide who caused the damage before reporting it. What you can do is connect the received item to its order, preserve the condition in which it arrived and explain exactly what you observed. A concise record gives support more to work with than a theory about where the damage began.
First establish when the problem became visible

A mark visible in a warehouse photo is a different situation from damage discovered after delivery. For a warehouse issue, save the picture and the item entry before asking for another view. For an issue on arrival, note the date of receipt, the parcel reference and the state in which you found the packaging. Use ordinary language such as “a crack visible at the upper joint of the handle.” If you only saw the crack after taking the mug out, say that. A clear chronology is more useful than pretending to have seen inside a sealed parcel.

Check the OOTDBuy Help Center promptly. Its warehouse and after-sales topics include damaged fragile items and issues found after receipt. Consult the current conditions shown for your order or parcel, particularly any reporting period or evidence requirement. Save a copy of the relevant instructions with your notes. A deadline mentioned in a forum for an unrelated shipment cannot establish how much time applies to yours. Start the inquiry while the package and its contents are still available to examine.
Preserve the relationship between item, box and protection

Start with one overview showing the item, outer package and internal packing together as you found them. Then take photographs that document one thing at a time. A view of the outside shows where the box was crushed or torn. A view of the internal supports shows how the item sat inside. A closer view of the handle identifies the affected component. Do not reconstruct a dramatic accident scene or bend the item further to make a mark easier to see. Describe any changes already made during opening.

If several orders share one parcel, include identifying details for the affected piece. A label on a retail box, an order option or a distinctive model number may connect it to the warehouse entry. Keep private order and parcel references in the support message. Before sharing a picture publicly for advice, consider what personal information the shipping label contains. The full label may be useful in a private case, but a public discussion rarely needs your address or tracking barcode.
Photograph the issue in context

A very close picture of a scratch can make it impossible to tell which object is shown. Take one image of the entire item from the affected side, another of the area and a close view if it reveals more detail. For glossy objects, change the angle of the light so that a reflection does not hide the line. Include a familiar scale beside the area if size matters, keeping both in the same plane. Avoid resting a heavy ruler on a fragile item.

With clothing, place the garment flat and show which seam or panel is affected. A picture that shows an open seam just below the left pocket is easier to interpret than a cropped image of loose thread on an unidentified surface. If the problem concerns a missing piece rather than a broken one, photograph everything you received together and show the paid option listing the expected components. A model wearing an accessory does not by itself establish that the accessory belonged to the selected purchase.
Reconstruct the records before writing the request

Collect the order confirmation, any relevant warehouse photos, the outbound parcel record and the delivery record. Write one sentence under each explaining what it establishes. The purchase record identifies the chosen version. The warehouse photograph shows the views taken at intake. The parcel record links the item to the shipment. The arrival pictures show the condition you could observe at home. There may be a gap between those stages, particularly where a component was hidden by wrapping.

A missing view is worth stating. If the warehouse images show the front of the mug but the crack is on the rear handle joint, write “the joint is outside the frame in the available warehouse pictures.” That is a stronger and fairer account than saying that the mug was definitely intact before dispatch. The same reasoning applies to a dented box. Report the dent and its location; let the case handler assess its relevance alongside the packing details and any carrier information.
Write a short, specific first message

A useful opening might read: “Parcel [reference] was delivered on [date]. It included the blue mug from order [reference]. On unpacking I found a crack at the upper handle joint. Attached are the parcel label, the outer carton, the internal packing, the complete mug and a close view of the crack. I still have the packaging. Please tell me which review process applies and whether you need another view.” Replace each placeholder with your own facts and attach the files you actually have.

When two units of the same item were in the order, say whether one or both are affected. If the case concerns a set, identify which piece failed and which pieces you can still use. It helps to say what outcome you are asking the platform to consider, such as reviewing replacement of one component. Distinguish that request from an entitlement. The available outcome depends on the applicable terms and the case evidence; your first message need not promise what the platform or carrier will decide.
Respond to follow-up requests without losing the original record

Keep the original images and send additional views as separate files. Name them in order or describe them in the message, especially when a support conversation crosses several days. If asked for a view that is no longer possible, explain why. Perhaps the delivery packaging was already opened before you saw the damage. A photograph taken after opening can still document the state of the item, provided it is presented accurately.

If a proposed remedy involves sending something back, check the written instructions before arranging a shipment. Confirm which pieces and packaging the recipient needs, who provides the return address and what record is required for the return. A parcel label from the original shipment is not necessarily an address for after-sales returns. If the proposed remedy is an account credit or partial refund, record its amount, currency and stated effect on the case before deciding whether it resolves the problem.
Close the file when the outcome is clear

Compare the final outcome with the request you actually made. If the platform said it would review one broken component, check that the resolution identifies that component and order. Save the case reference, decision and any confirmation of receipt or credit in one place. If the decision turns on a missing photograph or an unreadable label, record that specific lesson for your next parcel. You may find that one better overview at arrival would have saved several rounds of messages.

The best damage record is usually small enough to understand in a minute. It identifies the purchase, shows the relevant condition and preserves the sequence in which you learned about the problem. That makes it possible to ask a focused follow-up even when responsibility remains uncertain. For current reporting rules, follow the guidance in your OOTDBuy order and the official Help Center rather than relying on a generic template for every parcel.
What will an OOTDBuy find cost once item price and delivery are counted?

A spreadsheet price is useful for deciding which items deserve a closer look. Trouble begins when you treat that number as the amount required to receive the item at home. To plan an OOTDBuy purchase, build your total in stages. Keep the unit selected from the seller, the movement to the warehouse and the outbound parcel on separate lines. They happen at different times, can use different currencies and often apply to different groups of items.
Fix the purchase units before adding any delivery

Start with a list of exactly what you intend to buy. For each row record the seller, the option, its price in the displayed currency and the number of units. If a listing contains a set, name what one unit includes. A two-piece set ordered once is one seller unit and two physical pieces. Two single shirts ordered together are two seller units. This distinction matters when you compare a unit price, count received items or decide which parcel a later charge belongs to.

Consider an illustrative shopping list. You choose two shirts at 80 yuan each and one bag at 120 yuan. The item subtotal is 280 yuan. For now put that figure in a column labelled goods. Keep any accessory that you might add later on a separate draft line. Mixing alternatives with confirmed selections is an easy way to inflate your budget, while leaving an accessory out of a complete-set comparison can make one offer look cheaper than it really is.
Count seller-to-warehouse delivery once

Next, inspect the live purchase summary for domestic delivery. One seller may charge for an entire order; another may display a delivery amount on each line. Check the calculation shown for the combination you chose. In the example, suppose the two shirts share an eight-yuan domestic charge and the bag has a separate six-yuan domestic charge. Your purchase-stage total becomes 294 yuan before any other applicable payment or service charges. Charging eight yuan to each shirt would overstate the total by eight.

If a seller splits dispatch into two packages, the number of tracking numbers alone does not determine how many delivery charges you paid. Look at the actual order statement. Likewise, combining two marketplace purchases at the agent warehouse changes the outbound parcel, not the domestic payments already made. Keep domestic tracking numbers with the seller records and the international tracking number with the eventual parcel. It makes both your accounts and your delivery inquiries easier to follow.
Give the outbound parcel its own record

Create a row for the proposed parcel and list which purchases it contains. Add destination, route, packed weight and outer dimensions when known. Mark each value as measured or estimated. An estimate using a seller's product weight and an estimated box size has a different evidential basis from a quote based on a packed parcel. Preserve the inputs when you save a quote. The result alone cannot explain a later difference.

Suppose a calculator returns an illustrative 165 yuan for one particular set of inputs. That is a planning figure for the whole proposed parcel. Do not add 165 yuan to each item. Add it once to the purchase-stage total, giving a provisional 459 yuan in this example. If a packing option later costs 12 yuan, the revised planning total is 471 yuan. These are arithmetic examples, not OOTDBuy rates. Use the options available for your contents and destination, and confirm the amount shown before payment.
Compare routes using the same parcel

A change of route can affect the charge, eligible contents and delivery assumptions. To compare prices, keep the destination, units, weight and dimensions fixed. Note which services are included in each quote. A figure that includes an optional service cannot be compared fairly with a figure that omits the same service unless you explain the difference. If a route will not accept the parcel as described, mark it unavailable instead of treating its displayed price as a viable saving.

Size can matter as much as scale weight. A lightweight bag stuffed to preserve its shape may need a larger carton than the same bag packed flat. If the route considers dimensions when setting its billing weight, these are two different shipping scenarios. Ask how each would be packed and whether that method would protect the item. An attractive figure obtained by typing an unrealistically small box into a calculator does not tell you how much it will cost to send the parcel you actually want.
Allocate a shared cost only when it answers a real question

If you simply need the total cash commitment, stop at the parcel total. Allocation is useful when friends are splitting a shipment or you are comparing the delivered costs of individual pieces. Agree on the rule before paying. An equal split by seller unit is easy to explain, but two shirts and a bulky bag do not necessarily use equal space. Splitting by item value answers a different question again. None of these conventions changes what the carrier charges for the whole parcel.

In the example, an equal three-way allocation of the illustrative 165-yuan freight gives 55 yuan to each seller unit. Allocating by item value would assign each 80-yuan shirt about 47.14 yuan and the 120-yuan bag about 70.71 yuan before rounding adjustment. Those figures are bookkeeping choices. If the bag determines most of the box size, the group may prefer a separate comparison with and without the bag. Use one rule for settlement, record the rounding difference and ensure the shares add back to the actual parcel charge.
Handle currency without counting the conversion twice

Keep the original currency on every confirmed payment. If the spreadsheet displays a converted estimate, record the original price too. For a budget in your home currency, apply one stated planning rate to amounts in the same currency. Save the actual amount charged separately when your payment settles. An agent display rate, a payment provider's conversion and a card statement can describe different parts of the transaction. Do not apply a second currency conversion to an amount you already copied from your home-currency statement.

If you return an item, record the credit against the specific purchase and note where it was received. An account balance credit changes what you can spend through that account. It does not necessarily create an incoming transfer on the original card statement. Once an item leaves a planned parcel, recalculate the outbound scenario rather than assuming freight decreases by that item's original allocation. A different mix of pieces can still need the same carton or can qualify for a different route.
Reconcile the estimate after the final payment

Bring the purchase orders, packing selections and actual parcel charge back to your original sheet. Replace estimates in a new column so you can see why your budget changed. Identify whether each difference comes from the seller option, quantity, domestic delivery, optional packing, measured parcel, route or currency. If a final line is still unclear, send support the relevant reference and the two figures you are trying to reconcile. Asking about one charge on one record is easier to resolve than asking why the whole order felt expensive.

OOTDBuy's Help Center separates purchasing services and fees from delivery charges and packaging. Consult the relevant topic and the current checkout for transaction-specific terms. When those records agree, the spreadsheet has done its job. You can explain what you bought, what you paid to move it and how much remains an estimate. That is a much stronger basis for choosing the next find than comparing two attractive catalogue prices in isolation.
How to plan packaging for a mixed OOTDBuy parcel

A jacket, a narrow boxed accessory and a rigid bag may fit in the same shipping carton, but fitting is only one part of a packing decision. Before choosing a service, decide which shapes must survive, what can touch and what would become expensive or impossible to replace. A good request describes those conditions clearly enough that the warehouse can tell you whether its available packing options meet them.
Make an inventory of shapes and surfaces

Draw three columns on a piece of paper: item, vulnerable feature and acceptable change. For a jacket, the vulnerable feature might be a raised print that should not be creased sharply. For a bag, it might be a structured corner or a handle that needs support. For the accessory, the retail box might be part of a gift. A simple list of product names misses all three distinctions. Writing down the features helps you decide what original packaging can reasonably be removed.

Check the quantity and the intended destination of each piece. A compact accessory placed inside a bag can be easy to forget when parcel contents are checked. If an item belongs to a friend, find out whether that person wants the box, spare parts or protective cover. One buyer's unnecessary packaging may be another buyer's essential presentation box. Agree on those details before asking for anything to be discarded; an instruction to remove packaging is difficult to reverse after disposal.
Look for conflicts between the items

Imagine you put a metal buckle against an unprotected smooth bag. The buckle takes up little room, yet its edge may mark the larger piece if the contents shift. A hard rectangular retail box can push into a structured corner in the same way. The packing question is not simply which item is heavier. It is where the weight can concentrate and which surfaces can rub. Ask for separation around the vulnerable parts if the available service allows it.

Soft clothing can sometimes occupy unused space, but a soft item is not automatically suitable as protective material. A pale jacket next to an exposed dark surface, a garment with decorative studs, or a bulky item that presses a handle out of shape creates its own problems. If preserving a signature fold or a retail presentation matters, say so explicitly. Give the packer the goal, such as keeping hardware away from the coated face, instead of prescribing an elaborate arrangement the warehouse may be unable to offer.
Work out which retail packaging does useful work

Examine what the original box or insert does. An insert can hold a rigid handle in position, keep two pieces apart or keep a small component from vanishing. A larger outer sleeve might mainly add empty volume. Treat them as separate decisions. “Keep the shaped insert and the accessory pouch; the outer display sleeve can be removed if permitted” is more informative than “remove boxes.” If the warehouse offers only broad choices, ask what the selected option actually removes.

A pending exchange can change the decision. If an item is the wrong size or you have an unresolved inspection question, check the applicable return instructions before changing its packaging. Even when you plan to keep the item, a protected piece might be easier to inspect in its existing arrangement. Save an overview before approving an irreversible packing change if you need a record. For the packing services currently offered for the actual parcel, consult the Delivery and Packaging information in OOTDBuy and the choices shown at submission.
Compare two practical scenarios

Build one scenario that combines all eligible items and one that separates the piece with special needs. Record the destination, the items, the proposed protection and what measurements are known. If a route excludes an item or the resulting parcel exceeds an applicable size limit, remove that route from the comparison. There is little value in computing the cheapest version of a shipment that cannot use the selected service. Keep earlier estimates with their original date and assumptions.

As an illustration, suppose one proposed carton measures 40 by 30 by 20 centimetres. Its outside volume is 24,000 cubic centimetres. Adding five centimetres to the height changes that to 30,000, a 25 percent increase in volume. The actual weight might change very little. The price consequence depends on the line's billing rules, rounding and applicable limits. This example explains why dimensions deserve a place in your notes; it does not give an OOTDBuy rate, divisor or guaranteed saving from removing a box.
Ask for the information that changes the choice

If the decision turns on whether the bag travels upright or with its handle folded, ask that question directly. If it turns on freight, ask whether the dimensions you are comparing are estimated item dimensions or measured outer carton dimensions. Mixing those two produces a confident-looking comparison that answers very little. A useful request also lists what you are willing to change. The warehouse may be able to suggest a supported packing option once it knows which trade-offs are acceptable.

Here is a sample private order note: “Please keep the insert in the structured bag and the small accessory in its retail box. Please separate the buckle from the bag's coated front. The jacket may be folded, with the raised print kept flat if practical. If these items cannot be combined using the available service, please let me know before changing their retail packing.” Replace these details with your actual priorities. Do not include instructions that assume a particular service is free or guaranteed.
Review the submission screen as a parcel

Look at the warehouse references selected for the outbound parcel, especially when you own multiple versions of the same item. A recent replacement may have a different entry from the unit originally photographed. Check the address, delivery route, protection selections and any optional service charges together. Identify charges that apply to the whole carton and those attached to individual pieces. Save the confirmed selection with the item list so the final statement can be compared with the right scenario.

If a packed view is available, read it with the inventory beside you. Can you identify the rigid bag, the separate accessory and the jacket? Are any protective choices visible? A sealed-box view cannot tell you where the buckle sits. Treat the photograph according to what it shows and ask about a missing detail before dispatch if that detail would change your decision. A request for repeated pictures of an already sealed carton is unlikely to answer an internal placement question.
Keep a short unpacking record

When the parcel arrives, compare its label to your outbound reference. If something appears damaged, document the outer condition and internal protection as you uncover them. Keep the packaging while you consult the applicable after-sales instructions. If everything arrives as expected, write down what worked. A note such as “shaped insert preserved the bag; display sleeve was unnecessary for my use” is more transferable to your next mixed parcel than a bare freight total.

The most useful packing decision is one you can explain before and after the journey. You know which pieces are travelling together, which features deserve protection and which dimensions affect the quote. You have also made clear what may be removed and what needs your approval. With those details on record, a change in route or box size becomes a decision you can evaluate, instead of a surprise you discover after the parcel has gone.
How to trace the last delivery scan on an OOTDBuy parcel

Your order page says delivered, yet there is no parcel at your door. Before treating that as a failed delivery, find out which journey ended. A seller can deliver a purchase to an agent's warehouse well before an international parcel exists. An overseas carrier can also hand a shipment to another operator for the final address. A useful tracking note connects the latest event to the parcel, journey and operator it actually describes.
Start with the parcel you expected to receive

Open your OOTDBuy records and identify the international parcel containing the missing item. Check which warehouse items you selected for that parcel. If two garments were paid for together but submitted for delivery separately, the first parcel's tracking cannot answer where the second garment is. Write down the outbound parcel reference, route as displayed, destination country and carrier tracking reference. Keep your address and full tracking number inside your private notes and the official assistance channel.

If you cannot find an outbound parcel containing the item, check whether it is still a warehouse entry or awaiting a separate action on your part. A domestic tracking number from the seller may show a delivery at an address in China. That can be consistent with the purchase reaching the agent before you arrange its next journey. Compare the order record with the warehouse intake. If they do not reconcile, ask about the domestic delivery and provide the original order reference. An overseas carrier would have little to investigate at this stage.
Copy the latest event in its original wording

Open the tracking page of the carrier identified for your parcel. Copy the event wording, date, time and location exactly as shown. Also note when you checked and the name of the site reporting it. Keep a screenshot if the wording matters to a follow-up. An estimated delivery date at the top of a page is a forecast, while a timestamped event below it describes a recorded step. Save the two separately so a revised delivery estimate does not appear to overwrite an event.

Record a time zone when the page supplies one. An overseas scan shown in local facility time and an app notification stamped in the recipient's time can look out of order. If no zone is displayed, preserve the timestamp without converting it. The same applies to a city name: it can identify a facility that posted an update rather than the parcel's current physical position. A support question asking whether a handoff occurred after a named scan is more precise than asserting the parcel has been sitting in a particular building.
Follow the handoff using the carrier's own description

Look for a second tracking reference or a named delivery partner on the outbound parcel record. Keep the first reference beside it, labelled with its carrier. When the page supplies a partner number, open the named carrier's official tracking page and compare its events. A package can have an international movement record and a separate final-delivery record. A search result that recognises a number does not, by itself, prove that the site's suggested carrier is responsible for your parcel. An explicit connection in the shipping record is stronger evidence.

USPS, for example, distinguishes information received about a shipment from its own possession of the item. It also distinguishes an attempt from a completed delivery. Those distinctions can make sense of an apparent contradiction if USPS actually appears as the final carrier for your parcel. For a different route, use the named operator's explanation of the wording it displays. Keep its original wording if you translate the event for someone else. Two operators may use similar English phrases for different stages of a handoff.
Work through an example with two tracking numbers

Imagine an order containing a jacket and scarf. On Monday the jacket's seller reference ends with a domestic delivery scan. On Thursday the jacket and scarf appear together in one international parcel record with another reference. Later a destination operator reports that it has received electronic information about that parcel. These events describe three different observations. The first supports checking warehouse receipt of the jacket, the second identifies your requested outbound contents, and the third records a message in the destination carrier's network.

Now suppose the international carrier reports a handover, while the destination operator still shows only the initial electronic event. Preserve both dated messages. You can ask whether the named partner has a physical acceptance event or whether another reference was issued. You cannot settle that question by counting the number of days since the seller's Monday delivery. That scan belonged to the earlier domestic journey. Keeping the reference next to every event prevents an old successful delivery from masking a genuinely unresolved international handoff.
Read the action requested by the latest status

A pickup or attempted-delivery notice can require a different response from a parcel moving between facilities. Read the carrier's full message for the pickup location, redelivery options, required identification or action deadline, as applicable to the service shown. Reach the carrier through the tracking page or contact information you verified from its official site. If a text arrives asking for money or new address details, independently reopen the carrier's site before acting on it. A message containing a familiar parcel number can still be unrelated to an official delivery request.

If the event says delivered, compare the reported date and delivery location with your own circumstances. Check the normal receiving point, building reception or another location the carrier explicitly identifies. Ask other people who are authorised to receive your deliveries. Preserve any proof-of-delivery information the carrier makes available to you. Where the location remains unclear, state exactly what you checked when asking for assistance. Avoid publishing a delivery photograph, complete label or tracking reference on a public forum, where it can reveal information about the recipient.
Send an inquiry that can be followed from the first line

Start with one question and the identifiers needed to answer it. For example: your outbound parcel shows the international carrier's handoff event on the stated date, while the named destination carrier still shows an information-only event. Ask whether there is an updated final-mile reference or a physical acceptance record. Supply the private parcel reference, the carrier names and the relevant latest events. The official OOTDBuy help and contact pages are starting points for a question about the agent's own parcel record.

A request about a delivered parcel should identify the date and carrier location shown, the receiving points already checked and the fact that the recipient has not located it. Review the carrier's current instructions for reporting that particular status. Check the agent's applicable after-sales terms for any reporting window or evidence requirements. Keep these details with the specific parcel, since routes and services can differ. A generic promised wait or an assumed compensation amount could lead you to miss the instruction that actually applies to your shipment.
Close the timeline only when the outcome is clear

Track each reply by who provided it and what it established. A support case number confirms that someone opened an inquiry. A corrected final-mile reference can make a previously invisible tracking history available. A message that the carrier will investigate is still an open step. Keep the next expected action and any stated follow-up date beside the case. If a later scan arrives, add it beneath the previous one instead of replacing the record that prompted the inquiry.

When you receive the parcel, compare the label with the outbound reference and check the contents against the items assigned to it. If the parcel arrived but one garment is missing, close the delivery question and open a contents question with the relevant packaging and item evidence. If support confirms another outcome, retain the written resolution and identify precisely which parcel it covers. The result should let another reader tell which delivery was completed, which issue was investigated and whether any separate purchase is still in transit.
